figures.caption: Figure 1: The difference in scope between what general ontology and Foundry Ontology call "ontology"
figures.alt: Side-by-side comparison of what counts as “ontology.” Left: ontology in general (W3C standards), with a type layer (classes, properties, constraints; RDF, OWL, SHACL, SPARQL) and optional actual data (knowledge graph). Permissions and writes to business systems are outside the standards' scope. Right: Foundry Ontology (Palantir), where types, contents (objects and links), and components that make things happen (actions, functions, permissions) are all inside what Foundry calls “ontology.” A dotted line marks the two type layers as the same layer. Footer: not better or worse, a difference in how much gets called by the same name.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The same range declaration works as inference in OWL / RDFS and as validation in SHACL
figures.alt: Inference and validation do different jobs. A small graph of ep001 and ep002 (episodes) and guest001, with `features rdfs:range Person` and `sh:class Person / sh:minCount 1`. Left panel, without inference: guest001 is not stated as a Person and fails the class check; ep002 has zero guests and fails minCount. Right panel, with RDFS inference: guest001 is inferred as a Person from range, so that violation goes away; the minCount failure remains. Footer: OWL doesn't treat unstated facts as false (open-world assumption); write required checks in SHACL. Illustrative example, run with pySHACL 0.40.2.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Object types, link types, and properties (the type layer), and objects and links (the instance layer)
figures.alt: Types and instances are different layers. The upper plate is the type layer (object types, link types, properties): Theme, Episode, and Person, linked by ABOUT / covers and FEATURES / features, with properties publishedAt (publish date) and durationSeconds (length). This is close to “classes and properties” in ontology in general. The lower plate is the instance layer (objects and links): Theme: AI, Episode A, Episode B, Person X, Person Y. What is called a knowledge graph or object graph is mainly this layer. Episodes and people are fictional data.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The flow of an action: parameters → submission criteria → rules → writeback and side effects → action log
figures.alt: An action defines how things get changed. Six steps: ① Parameters (input types); ② Submission criteria (who, and in what state; can be submitted only when all are met); ③ Rules (create, modify, delete objects and links / function rules); ④ Applied in a single transaction; ⑤ Writeback and side effects (writeback dataset, business systems / notifications, webhooks); ⑥ Action log (records successful submissions only). A rejection branch from step ②: not met → cannot submit (failures are tracked in action metrics). A permissions rail: roles / object and property policies (cell-level). The author’s view: this whole set of constraints is a “harness” (not a Palantir term). Example: change a flight's aircraft — only if the user is in the flight controllers group and the aircraft is in service.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Structure of the research repository: collecting public data → schema → graph and aggregation → demos (fictional data) → verification
figures.alt: Inside the research repository pivot-ontology. Top row, public data: ① Collect (public data from PIVOT's official YouTube channel); ② Normalize (Episode / MetricsSnapshot); ③ Extract (rules / LLM); ④ Schema (schema.yaml, with provenance: public, owner, derived, computed, external); ⑤ Graph and aggregates (the 212 episodes that are “fully collected AND public for 30+ days”). Below, a simulation on fictional data: Demo 1 operational-ontology-demo (operations spanning four business systems; cancel and return as separate actions); Demo 2 pivot-live-studio (a real Codex agent + human approval); Demo 3 pivot-team-agent-demo (the demo used on the show; runs to a script). At right, pivot-ontology-basis for verification (A plain text / B glossary / C ontology / Z no knowledge; unpublished, not peer-reviewed). Legend: public data, synthetic data, evaluation data.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Where the LLM agent sits: it reads the ontology, proposes changes, and nothing is finalized until those changes pass human approval and the submission criteria
figures.alt: AI proposes, humans approve. An LLM agent (Codex) sits on an ontology plate (definitions of types, relationships, actions) and uses ontology_schema, search_objects, traverse_graph, and get_object. The flow, left as drawn: change plan (proposal) — propose_rebooking; human approval — approve_plan (production lead only; not among the agent's tools); pre-execution check — check_plan (have the premises (versions) changed since approval?); commit — commit_rebooking (applied in one transaction); audit record (keeps both successes and refusals). A dotted loop: premises changed → can't commit → redo the plan. Footer: conditions for execution and who approves are bound by server-side definitions, not by the prompt. Fictional data; no Palantir products are used.

figures.caption: Figure 7: The difference in size between the effect of providing knowledge and the effect of writing that knowledge in ontology form
figures.alt: What helps first is providing knowledge. Four bars, as points of difference vs. no knowledge or vs. plain text: whether knowledge is provided, +25.7 to +49.3; same knowledge in ontology form (high difficulty, main analysis), +2.3 (significant); same (conservative re-analysis), ≈ +2.0 (not significant after correction); procedural work (Experiment II), −0.5 (no significant difference). Footer: unpublished, not peer-reviewed; results from a single fictional business; analysis covers 2,117 runs.
